# Build Log

[Documentation index](../README.md) · [Build plan](BUILD-PLAN.md) · [Architecture specification](../architecture/ARCHITECTURE.md)

## Format

This is a chronological session log so a future session (or a different contributor) can resume work without reconstructing context from scratch. It is not a substitute for the ADRs, the research records, or BUILD-PLAN.md; it links to them rather than restating their content.

The **Current state** block at the top of this file is overwritten each session: it always describes the repository as of the most recent session, not a history of how it got there. History lives in the dated entries below it, appended in reverse chronological order (newest first).

### Session entry template

```
## YYYY-MM-DD

**Goal:** what this session set out to do.

**Completed:** what was actually finished, with file paths.

**Decisions made:** any decision recorded, and where (ADR number, research record, or this log if it doesn't rise to either).

**Questions raised with the owner:** question and answer, if any came up.

**Deferred:** anything deliberately left for later, and why.

**Verification gates:** state of tests, CI, and any acceptance criteria from BUILD-PLAN.md touched this session. Only report gates actually run this session.
```

## Current state

> **OPEN, and the first thing to settle on 2026-08-14: deployment identity in test fixtures.** The repository is public. Prose documentation was redacted in `b149663`, but hostnames and IP addresses from the operator's network remain in test fixtures and test code. **The owner's constraint is that there must be a solution in which hostnames and IPs do not appear in those files in any form.** He explicitly did not accept the options offered on 2026-08-13 and did not want the question resolved that evening, so **this is recorded without a recommendation and a future session should not adopt the earlier framing by default.**
>
> **Where it is:** `internal/coordinator/collector/fpp/testdata/*.json` (60K), `internal/coordinator/collector/fppmqtt/testdata/*.json` (56K), `internal/coordinator/config/config_test.go`, and `ui/src/app/test-support/fppFleetFixtures.ts`. Roughly 100 references, and assertions key off the hostnames.
>
> **Facts a decision needs.** Six test files across four packages read those fixtures, so untracking them without another mechanism breaks the suite on a fresh clone and in CI. The fixtures are captures from the live 2026-08-11 probe, and their value is FPP's real response *shape*: the heterogeneous ports array, `"ma": null`, the `warnings` key absent on one host while its MQTT topic publishes `[]`. Each of those broke a decoder and each is a recorded lesson, so whatever replaces them has to preserve shape. Editing a file labelled as a verbatim capture without saying so is its own problem. Git history still contains every identifier regardless of what happens next, and scrubbing that means a rewrite and force-push on a public default branch, which nobody has agreed to.
>
> **Angles not yet examined**, listed so tomorrow starts with more than two options, and **not** as recommendations: generating fixtures at test time from a redacted template; stripping identity fields in the test helper at load; storing only the fields under test rather than whole responses; keeping captures out of git with CI synthesizing equivalents.


Steps 0 (Foundation), 1 (`pkg/multisync`), 2 (control plane skeleton), 3 (read-only FPP observability plus the versioned public API), 4 (the read-only Operator UI), 5 (real FPP signals on the dashboard), 6 (identity, authorization and audit), 7 (the first three write operations), and **8 (the primitive command vocabulary)** are complete.

**Step 8 gave ShowMesh a vocabulary instead of a single verb.** Eight primitives — `startPlaylist`, `stopPlaylist`, `stopPlaylistGracefully`, `pausePlaylist`, `resumePlaylist`, `nextPlaylistItem`, `prevPlaylistItem`, `setVolume` — each confirmed through a signal the collector already collects, on evidence that post-dates its own dispatch. **This is the first step whose direction reverses**: `startPlaylist` is the first thing ShowMesh can do whose failure mode is the display running when it should not be.

**The capture came first, and that ordering paid for itself immediately.** [docs/bench/fpp-command-vocabulary.md](../bench/fpp-command-vocabulary.md) records FPP 9.5.3's real command list, its real argument encoding, and its real behaviour, taken from the bench `fppd` before any command was named. It overturned four assumptions that read as entirely plausible. **FPP's `200` means its command dispatcher ran and nothing more**: `Start Playlist` against a playlist that does not exist answers `200 "Playlist Starting"` and the host stays idle, and Pause, Resume, Next and Prev all answer cheerfully while idle and do nothing. **`ifNotRunning` is not the guard its name promises** — it suppresses restarting the *same* playlist and does nothing to protect a different running show. **`Next Playlist Item` at the last item ends the playlist**, so "skip" and "stop" are the same command one press from the end. **A graceful stop cannot confirm on `idle` within any deadline ShowMesh can choose**, because its terminal state is bounded by the current item's runtime, measured holding `stopping gracefully` indefinitely against a 120-second item. And `Test Start` segfaulted `fppd`, taking the whole FPP web API down until the container was restarted.

**43 of the 51 captured commands are not shipped, and each exclusion is recorded with its reason** in that document's own register, split by who owns the gap: signals ShowMesh does not yet collect, effects FPP does not expose at all, and a third group the capture forced — commands excluded by ShowMesh's own rules, like the relative volume commands whose replay would compound, and `Toggle Playlist`, whose desired state is unknowable before dispatch and so has nothing to record under ADR-003.

**The design question was answered rather than discovered.** A start issued against a host already playing something else **refuses by default**. `ifBusy` carries `refuse` (the default, and what an absent field means) and `replace`. FPP's own answer is to silently swap the show; ShowMesh's is not. The guard is evaluated against evidence that can be stale, so it is a guard and not a lock, and it refuses rather than proceeding when it cannot tell.

**Confirmation now takes about half a second, and the fence is unchanged.** The command reached FPP in milliseconds while confirmation waited out the collector's 15-second cadence, so an action that completed instantly reported back in 0 to 15 seconds. A post-dispatch poll nudge asks the collector to poll that instance immediately. Measured live: **13–15 s down to 0.55–0.61 s**. What counts as evidence did not move: a nudged poll produces an ordinary observation, resolved through `ResolveObservations` and fenced on `CollectedAt` exactly as before, and `resumePlaylist` against an idle host still runs out its full 20-second deadline and reports `unconfirmed`. The nudge is rate limited per instance so a macro in Step 9 cannot become a poll storm against a show host.

**Six things a future session should know before touching this code.** They are in LESSONS.md; the two that cost the most are below.

**The confirmation defect returned, and the person who wrote the rule against it introduced it.** `nextPlaylistItem` accepted `idle` as confirmation, correctly, because Next at the last item ends the playlist. It never checked the host was not *already* idle. So the exact input the capture had already measured — Next while idle, `200 "Next Item Playing"`, nothing happens — reported `confirmed`. Found by running it against the bench, not by any test; the test that named that branch was itself a coin flip, passing on a race between bcrypt principal creation and a fixed 60 ms sleep. The baseline now captures status as well as index, and the idle branch is unavailable without a current, non-idle pre-dispatch reading.

**A comment is a claim, and a comment claiming a test is the worst kind.** Two shipped in this step, both of them the *fix* for an earlier defect. The browser's command timeout carried a doc comment saying a test proved it; no such test existed, and lowering the constant below the server's deadline left 389 tests, typecheck, lint and build all green. The handler's doc comment said `stopPlaylist` was the only member of ADR-024 decision 11's safety class while the code exempted all eight, so `startPlaylist` would dispatch with degraded attribution when the audit store failed. Decision 11 exists so a *stop* is never refused for want of an audit write; a start refused under the same condition costs only that the show does not start, which is the safe direction. `fppPrimitive.SafetyClass` is now a three-valued enum whose zero value fails the build, so "nobody decided" cannot masquerade as "decided no".

**Operator-facing copy is a surface with its own defect class.** The first shipped strings cited repo paths at the operator: a UI warning ended with `(docs/bench/fpp-command-vocabulary.md section 3.5)`. Found by the owner loading the real page. Two guard tests now fail on any repo path, `.md` reference, ADR number or `section N` in an operator-facing string, one walking the Go AST and one walking the TypeScript AST. What the operator reads and what a maintainer needs to know are different documents.

**What Step 8 does not do.** There is still no reconciler closing desired and observed state, because that loop is ShowMesh becoming a second scheduler. There are no macros, so ADR-024 decision 7's fallback trigger remains outstanding and still attaches to the first consumer of `show:macro:run`. Nothing here verifies anything about a running show: every FPP interaction was against `bench/fpp-multisync`'s containerized `fppd`, never the deployed fleet, whose command lists this capture does not describe — §6 establishes the command list is assembled at runtime per host, not fixed by version. **The Operator UI's command controls work and are not designed**; the owner's verdict after a real browser pass was that the states are correct and the visual design needs its own pass, which belongs to OBSERVABILITY.md rather than to this step. **Operator-facing error copy is improved and not finished**, recorded as a deferral rather than a completed item: the repo-path citations are gone and guarded against, but the messages remain longer and more technical than an operator wants mid-show. Nothing in this step is release-ready, and both of these are cheaper to finish once alongside the surface work than piecemeal here.

**Step 7 is done, and ShowMesh can now change something.** Three writes: the configuration surface that moved `SHOWMESH_FPP_ENDPOINTS` into the store (RES-008 D1), node discovery and declaration (D2), and one native FPP lifecycle command. Every one requires an authenticated principal holding the named scope; reads stay open by default, because a credential problem must never cost the operator sight of the show.

**The command is FPP's own `Stop Now`, and two things the plan asserted about it were wrong.** FPP has no command called `Stop Playlist`; the zero-argument member of its stop family is `Stop Now`, and `Stop Gracefully` takes a `loop` argument. The confirmation signal is `fpp.status` carrying `status_name`, not `fpp.status.player_state`. Both read as plausible until something ran against the bench daemon. `stopPlaylist` remains ShowMesh's own action name on its own wire, which is a deliberate distinction rather than an inconsistency.

**Five things a future session should know before touching this code.**

**Confirmation must rest on evidence collected after the dispatch.** The first implementation compared the current observation to the desired value and never checked its age relative to the command, while observations stay `current` for 45 seconds. Measured live: a dispatched command reported `confirmed` **179 microseconds** after `dispatchedAt`, far too fast to have re-polled anything. Since FPP is the authoritative scheduler and starts playlists on its own, that means a stop dispatched into a running show could report success off a pre-dispatch `idle` reading. ADR-003 asks for evidence that observed state *moved*, and "the value currently equals what I wanted" is not that. The same command now takes ten seconds, because it waits for a real poll.

**A client that gives up before the server answers deletes an outcome from existence.** The server holds an unconfirmed response for its full 20 second deadline; the CLI defaulted to 10 seconds and the browser to 15, so `unconfirmed` was unreachable by both shipped clients and the operator was told a transport failure for a successful conversation with a healthy coordinator. That is ADR-024 decision 7's inversion, in its fourth recorded variant. Client budgets are now derived from the server's deadline, with a test that fails if one is ever set below it.

**Confirmation reads through `ResolveObservations`, never the first matching row.** Two collectors emit `fpp.status` for the same resource and the observations primary key includes `source`, so taking the first row was a coin flip that could report unconfirmed against fresh REST evidence, or confirm falsely off a retained MQTT value. `precedence.go` already owned this rule and its own doc comment claimed resolving once there made the rule impossible to apply inconsistently. It was being applied inconsistently one file over.

**`complete: true` on a discovery run is the licence to assert absence, so it must be earned.** A run treated `LivenessUnknown` as "not observed" and finished complete regardless, so a 40 second broker outage, or a coordinator restart before retained state arrived, would flip every declared node in the installation to `not_seen`. `LivenessOffline` is real evidence and still supports `not_seen`; ambiguous evidence now finishes the run incomplete with a stated reason. This is the same rule as Step 5's "only a complete poll may prune", now decided for a fourth subsystem.

**A JSON absent key is still not an empty value, and this step shipped it twice.** A configuration `PUT` with no `endpoints` key wiped every endpoint and returned `200`; a second `declare` with no label erased the operator's label. Both are the Step 5 `"ma": null` lesson at a different layer. Absent, `null`, and explicitly empty are now three distinct things on both surfaces.

**One Step 7 finding was fixed on 2026-08-13, and it is a fifth thing worth knowing.** The `SHOWMESH_FPP_ENDPOINTS` to store migration failed closed on its audit write, so an unwritable `audit_log` meant the coordinator exited 1, which under the bundle's `restart: unless-stopped` is a restart loop with no API and no dashboard. **Fail-closed on attribution protects the operator from an unaccountable actor, and a startup migration has no principal**, so refusing it protected nobody while costing everything. It now logs at ERROR, persists nothing, collects from the environment's list exactly as it did before, and retries next boot, for both the audit-write and the revision-write failure modes. That exempts nothing from ADR-024 decision 11, because the transaction still rolls back, which is why it needed no ADR change. Proved against a real binary with a real unwritable `audit_log`: `HEAD` exits 1, the fix stays up and persists nothing.

**And the fix's own review found the sharper half.** Removing the exit made a state reachable that had been impossible, so two surfaces were left asserting things that were now false: the configuration read handler reported that nothing had ever been configured while the dashboard listed every host being polled, and the write refusal's remedy told the operator to remove `SHOWMESH_FPP_ENDPOINTS` and restart, which in that state discards the only copy of the endpoint list. **When you turn a fatal path into a survivable one, enumerate what becomes reachable and re-read what every existing surface says about it**; a remedy written for the normal case is the most dangerous text in the system, because operators execute it. Both are fixed and both were re-proved against a real coordinator with a real administrator and token. Full detail in the 2026-08-13 entry, including a test written in the same commit that asserted the right thing against the wrong string and passed under mutation.

**What Step 7 does not do.** There is no reconciler closing the gap between desired and observed state, and `desired_state`'s own comment says why: that loop is ShowMesh becoming a second scheduler, which ADR-001 forbids. There are no macros, so ADR-024 decision 7's fallback trigger is still outstanding and still attaches to the first consumer of `show:macro:run`. A configuration change does not hot-reload; a restart is required, and the API response and the UI both say so at the point of use. And nothing here verifies anything about a running show: every FPP interaction in this step was against `bench/fpp-multisync`'s containerized `fppd`, never the deployed fleet, because `falcon/player/<host>/command/run` is a topic FPP acts on.

**The next action is Step 9, show macros and the FPP plugin, and it is fully unblocked.** Its RES-008 prerequisite was discharged on 2026-08-13 and its one open scope question was answered the same day: the first macros ship with **no critical local fallback**, stated in each macro definition rather than left implicit, because the delivery path needs the ADR-025 agent cache plus an ADR-008 topic and both are cut from day-0.

**Work is no longer a single sequence of steps.** BUILD-PLAN's "Delivery tracks and the day-0 schedule" section, added 2026-08-13, runs five tracks in parallel: **A** is FPP control (Steps 8 and 9), **B** nodes and projection, **C** the audio node, **D** Resolume control and timecode, **E** show authoring and assets. Steps 8 and 9 are Track A; the numbered steps were kept and not renumbered.

**Day-0 is mid-September 2026** and the Halloween show opens **17 October**. Scope at day-0 is the whole show rather than an FPP slice. **Three founding problems decide what may never be cut**: generating virtual matrix data (Track B), controlling Resolume (Track D), and FPP's scheduler (Track A). Each alone is why this project was started.

**Ten records were written on 2026-08-13** alongside Step 8: ADR-026 (renderer surface model and NDI as reference transport), ADR-027 (show and surface model), ADR-028 (asset store, and a filename is not an asset identity), ADR-029 (macros invoke logical actions, never protocol commands), ADR-030 (the Operator UI as authoring surface), plus RES-003 raised to L1 on the FPP Connect compatibility surface, RES-008's section 3 re-surveyed at schema v6, and owner decisions folded into RES-001, RES-006 and RES-007.

**RES-008 section 3 was re-surveyed against schema v6 on 2026-08-13**, discharging Step 9's prerequisite. It reversed the 2026-08-12 survey's central finding, since configuration, revision, desired-state and command tables all now exist, and it established that **macro storage needs no schema migration**: `config_objects` and `config_revisions` are keyed `(kind, id)` with a JSON payload, so a macro definition is a new `kind` plus a payload schema. The 2026-08-12 survey is preserved as section 3a because sections 4 and 6a were written against it.

**It also found one thing that blocked Step 9's specification, since resolved above, and it is worth keeping because the reasoning carries into the macro work.** ADR-004 requires every critical macro to define a reduced local fallback, and there is currently **no path by which one could reach a node**: the agent has no cached fallback subset, ADR-025 decided that mechanism's trust model and Step 7 built none of it, and ADR-008's v1 topic set has no configuration-distribution topic. So either Step 9 builds the distribution path alongside the plugin, or the first macro is deliberately scoped to one with no critical fallback and says so. The second is likely right and is the shape Step 7 used, but it has to be decided rather than defaulted into.

**Step 8 was something else until 2026-08-13, and the correction is worth knowing.** (Historical, and the reason the numbering reads the way it does.) This block, CLAUDE.md, and the build order all named Step 8 as the agent's GStreamer pipeline supervision into an NDI sink, while BUILD-PLAN's own "not yet sequenced" section listed that identical work as blocked on RES-004 (unresearched, L0), RES-005 (unresearched, L0), and RES-006 (L1). Three documents pointed at a step the fourth said could not start, and the fourth was the status authority. It is now sequenced after the bench that raises those records, because it is a step whose product is evidence rather than shipped supervision code.

Primitives come before macros for a reason Step 7 supplies the evidence for: a macro is a sequence of primitives, exactly one exists, and if macros went first the primitives would get built inside that step. Step 7 was specified as one write and shipped three for the same reason. Two decisions were settled on 2026-08-13 before Step 8 could be specified, both recorded in its BUILD-PLAN section: **target-scoped authorization is declined rather than deferred**, so ADR-024's supersession trigger firing in Step 9 is a question already answered rather than a gap; and **`fpp:command` stays one scope**, because `operator` means the principal operates the show and starting it is operating it.

Also available and unchanged in priority: RES-002's bench capture and `pkg/pjlink` at L1.

Step 5 detail follows.

**Step 5 is the first work in this project exercised against real show hardware.** The coordinator was run read-only against all three deployed FPP hosts and the operator's live MQTT broker, and every acceptance criterion was demonstrated there rather than only in a fixture. What that does and does not license is in the Step 5 entry below; the short version is that it proves shape, type and modelling against *these* versions, and proves nothing about a running show. RES-002 stays L2 for protocol semantics and L1 for anything hardware-dependent, unchanged. **RES-011 is not raised**: every `ma` on the fleet reads 0 because the display is de-energized.

There are now two collectors behind one interface. `internal/coordinator/collector/fpp` polls the REST API of each configured instance; `internal/coordinator/collector/fppmqtt` subscribes read-only to FPP's own MQTT status topics on the operator's existing broker. They report overlapping signals on purpose, and `internal/coordinator/api/precedence.go` resolves them by a documented rule at read time. Storage is schema v4, whose primary key gained `source` so neither collector can silently overwrite the other's evidence.

**Four things a future session should know before touching this code.**

**GET-only is not read-only.** The collector never issues a non-GET, and that guarantee turned out to be nearly worthless on its own: FPP invokes commands over GET at `/api/command/...`, and neither HTTP client set `CheckRedirect`, so a 302 from a spoofed or compromised FPP would have walked the coordinator's own GET onto another host's command endpoint. Reproduced against a recorder before it was fixed. `CheckRedirect` is now forced onto a defensive copy of whatever client is in play, including a caller-supplied one, and a 3xx surfaces as `collection_failed`.

**A JSON `null` is not an absent key, and every extractor treated it as one.** `encoding/json` unmarshals `null` as a no-op returning no error, so `"ma": null` produced a measured `0 milliamps` on a smart-receiver position, `"powerBad": null` produced `false` and contributed *healthy*, and `"warnings": null` fabricated "no warnings". The blind-spot rule had been implemented for a missing key and not for a key present as null. Every extractor now rejects an explicit null.

**Health had to change before these signals could land, and it hid a fault while it was at it.** Every observation was a critical member of the instance verdict, so the many legitimately `unsupported` signals this step adds would have pinned all three real hosts at `unknown` forever. Worse, the mapper never looked at a value, only at whether the state was `current`, so `fpp.power.bad == true` contributed *healthy*. Now `unsupported` contributes nothing, only `fpp.reachable`, `fpp.fppd.state` and `fpp.power.bad` are health-critical, and a `healthy` verdict additionally requires `fpp.fppd.state` to be present and reading `running`, because "the HTTP server answered" is not evidence that the player is well.

**The change stream carried an entire instance to report a four-field delta, and that is now fixed** by [ADR-023](../decisions/ADR-023-change-stream-observation-deltas.md), measured on the live fleet at **46.3 KB/s down to 1.0 KB/s, a 44x reduction**. Deltas are opt-in per connection (`?deltas=1`) so the change is additive under ADR-020; the UI opts in and `showmeshctl` can exercise it. The two frame kinds have **opposite merge semantics**, which is the sharp edge: `fpp.changed` carries the complete observation set and is a replacement, `fpp.observations.changed` is a merge plus a `removed` list. Getting that backwards fails silently in both directions and is why ADR-023 decision 3a spells it out.

**Observations are now pruned**, so a swapped cape no longer leaves ghost port rows. `Collector.Poll` returns `(observations, complete bool)` and only a complete delivery may prune; a backed-off poll claims nothing, because deleting a source's evidence the first time it backs off would be far worse than a stale ghost.

Step 4 detail follows.

There is now an operator-facing surface. `ui/` is a React and Vite TypeScript SPA served from its own `nginx:alpine` container, which also forwards `/api/*` to the coordinator so the browser sees one origin ([ADR-022](../decisions/ADR-022-operator-ui-serves-the-api-same-origin.md)). It renders the dashboard, node and capability views, FPP instances, and event history, all composed from advertised capabilities rather than fixed node classes. Its API types are generated from `api/openapi.yaml` and CI fails on any diff, which makes ADR-015's "generated from or verified against the Go types" a gate rather than an intention: the OpenAPI document is already conformance-tested against real handler responses in both directions.

**Three things a future session should know before touching the UI.**

**A test environment that differs from the deployment environment reports success on exactly that difference.** The client invoked `fetch` as `this.fetchImpl(...)`, so its receiver was the client instance. A browser's `fetch` is a WebIDL operation on `Window` and answers any other receiver with `Illegal invocation`; Node's does not check. The app could not make a single request in Chrome while 99 unit tests passed, including the ones driving a real `node:http` server. Three reviews and a build of the shipped image did not find it. Loading the page did, immediately.

**Ages must keep advancing when responses stop.** Evidence ages were computed against the last response's `serverTime` as a fixed "now", so with the coordinator stopped for 100 seconds the banner and the last-updated notice correctly reported the disconnection while the evidence panel still read `current` and "observed just now". Ages now advance from the last `serverTime` by real elapsed browser time, which keeps clock skew visible while making elapsed time true, and evidence carries an explicit as-of qualifier while disconnected. The coordinator's `state` verdict is deliberately left untouched: it has provenance, and the UI inventing its own is what ADR-011 forbids.

**`env_file` loads every variable in the file, not the ones you named.** The UI service declared only two environment variables and inherited `SHOWMESH_API_TOKEN` and the broker password alongside them, readable through `docker inspect`. Three separate comments in the bundle asserted that the container never holds the token. ADR-022 decision 2 forbids *holding* it, not merely injecting it as a header, because holding it makes reaching the UI equivalent to reaching the API. Compose still interpolates `${VAR}` from `.env` without `env_file`, so removing it cost nothing.

Timeouts, backoff bounds, idle deadlines, retained-event caps, and the clock-skew warning threshold in the UI are unmeasured ShowMesh hypotheses, labelled as such in code, and belong to RES-009 and RES-013 along with their coordinator-side counterparts.

Step 3 detail follows.

The coordinator now polls configured FPP instances read-only over REST, normalizes what it finds into the OBSERVABILITY §4.1 observation model with provenance and freshness, persists observations and an event history in SQLite, and serves all of it through a versioned public API at `/api/v1` with a Server-Sent Events change stream. `showmeshctl` is a second, deliberately independent client of that API: an enforced import-graph test forbids it from importing any coordinator package, so a JSON tag rename breaks it rather than silently renaming the field on both sides. `api/openapi.yaml` is the machine-readable contract and is conformance-tested against real handler responses in both directions.

At the time of Step 3 there were no commands and no write operations of any kind, which stayed true until Step 7. Step 4 supplied the UI, and its version negotiation is now exercised for real against a coordinator that refuses the client's version.

RES-002 stays **L2 for protocol semantics** and **L1 for anything hardware- or network-dependent**, unchanged by this step. Step 3 added REST-level evidence about FPP (recorded in RES-002's evidence section) but nothing about the MultiSync wire protocol, the hardware clock, or the reference switch. L2 licenses further building, not a live show.

Three things a future session should know before touching this code. **`MultiSyncEnabled` defaults to off in FPP**, and the endpoint that looks like it reports that setting returns the setting's *schema*, which decodes to `false` without error: correct today by accident, wrong the moment MultiSync is enabled, and its test passes either way. The collector reads the running daemon's own `multisync` flag instead, and a test panics if anything ever calls the settings endpoint. **A retained MQTT delivery carries no valid observation time**, so `observedAt` is `null` with state `unknown_age` and must never be filled in from the collection time; that defect has now been introduced and caught three times in different disguises. And **`offline` means the control-plane connection is gone**, not that the node is dead, which is why the wire field is `node.controlPlane.state` and nothing else.

The heartbeat interval, staleness window, poll cadences, backoff bounds, SSE keepalive interval, and event retention bounds are all unmeasured ShowMesh hypotheses, labelled as such in code. They belong to RES-009 and RES-013.

`pkg/multisync` holds the MultiSync wire codec, a listener that receives multicast, broadcast, and unicast on UDP 32320, a timeline state machine implementing FPP remote semantics on an injectable clock, and an opt-in discover-ping responder. `cmd/showmesh-multisync-probe` is the bench instrument built to close RES-002's five open items; it has not been run against a real FPP player yet, so RES-002 remains at L1 and its status is still `planned`. Changing that status is the owner's call once real captures exist, per `docs/bench/RES-002-capture-procedure.md`.

Step 0 detail follows.

Step 0 (Foundation) is complete and verified. The repository builds, tests, and lints clean; the coordinator image builds for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` and runs; the Compose bundle brings up Mosquitto and the coordinator together and the coordinator reaches ready. The coordinator survives an unreachable broker, a broker stopped and restarted underneath it, and SIGTERM in every one of those states. There is no show logic, no MQTT topic work, and no persistence yet: `/healthz`, `/readyz`, and `/version` are the entire surface.

The repository is pushed to `github.com/ShowMeshSystems/showmesh`, which was private at the time of this entry and is **public as of 2026-08-14**, and CI has run on a real GitHub runner. It earned its keep on the first run by failing a test that passes on macOS, which is what exposed the `SO_REUSEADDR` behavior difference recorded in ADR-013.

No audio code exists. The Audio Engine was specified in the same session (ADR-017..019, `docs/architecture/AUDIO-ENGINE.md`, RES-007 rewritten) and deliberately left unsequenced: RES-007 is critical-risk at L0, the multichannel interface has not been purchased, and every load-bearing claim is a bench fact. The next audio action is the RES-007 prototype, not implementation.

The operator surface has now been checked on a real phone and a real desktop browser: the pixel-current blind-spot distinction holds, and the Step 4 sidebar defect is gone. Two things are deliberately deferred rather than forgotten: **the whole-UI styling pass**, still parked at the end by the owner's Step 4 decision, and **the observation list's readability**, which was raised by that phone check and filed with the styling work rather than patched.

**Step 6 is complete, and Step 7 is now specified.** [ADR-024](../decisions/ADR-024-identity-authorization-and-audit.md) was written on 2026-08-11 and implemented on 2026-08-12 by five parallel seams, then attacked by three reviews and repaired. It supersedes ADR-021 and ADR-022 decision 4.

Step 7 carried **three writes rather than one**: a primitive FPP lifecycle command, the configuration write surface, and node discovery. No macro. Both Step 6 obligations closed in its seam 0: `identity.Service` gained an atomic audit variant, and login CSRF was decided strictly and amended into ADR-024 decision 6.

**The reason Step 7 grew is worth knowing before anyone tries to shrink it back.** ADR-024 decision 11 carries two distinct audit rules. A **coordinator-local** state change writes its audit entry in the same transaction; a command **dispatched outward** writes its entry before dispatch. The same-transaction rule is the one Step 6 could not achieve and that must close first, and **a device command never exercises it.** Configuration and discovery writes are exactly its shape. So the coordinator-local writes prove the atomicity fix and the FPP command proves ADR-003 confirmation by evidence, and neither can cover the other's rule.

**A day of research on 2026-08-12 moved RES-008 and RES-015 to L1 and changed three things.** Full detail in the session entry below; the parts that alter the plan are here.

**Decision 7 cannot be discharged in FPP's native command mechanism, and ADR-024's argument for it was wrong in a new way.** That record reasons from an asymmetry: a coordinator outage is a transport failure *which is what a fallback detects and fires on*, while a `403` fires nothing. Source-verified at FPP `9.4`, `9.5.3` and `master`, and re-verified during fold-in: `CURLINFO_RESPONSE_CODE` appears **zero times** on every ref, so a `401` is indistinguishable from a `200`; and on the deployed `9.4` and `9.5.3`, `isError()` tests handle setup only, so **a refused connection also reports success.** Neither failure fires anything, because FPP detects neither. The conclusion survives and the obligation grows: transport-failure detection must be built too, and all of it lives in ShowMesh code on the FPP host. **That puts RES-015 on the macro step's critical path rather than beside it.** The generalizable shape is a third variant of one defect: decision 7 was written to correct an argument made against the wrong failure *direction*, and this is an argument made against a failure-detection *capability assumed rather than checked*.

**A credential on an FPP host must be treated as public.** FPP publishes every command's arguments in cleartext to `command/run`, writes config `0664`, streams any config file over `/api/configfile/**` with no allowlist, is unauthenticated by default, and redacts backups by an exact key-name list holding only `emailpass`, `password`, `secret` on the deployed versions. The accepted posture is now explicit in `SECURITY.md`: **cleartext on the isolated show LAN is fine for commands, macros, status and telemetry, and is never acceptable for a credential**, because a leaked secret outlives the packet and is replayable. FPP's native `URL` command sets no header on any version, so the only place a credential could go is the URL, which then gets published. It is therefore unusable for an authenticated call, which is the second independent reason the macro step ships a plugin. Improving FPP's own posture is upstream work and explicitly out of scope.

**[ADR-025](../decisions/ADR-025-agent-fallback-cache-is-signed.md) settles the agent cache's trust model**, superseding ADR-009's `checksummed`. Two accepted documents had disagreed behind the shared word *verified*. Signing creates a trust anchor, and the anchor collided with a constraint ADR-024 had already recorded: **the cache exists for the case where the coordinator is unreachable, so a key fetched at boot would fail exactly when needed.** Resolved by pinning the verifying key at enrollment, which is operator-initiated and therefore happens while the coordinator is up. Two findings from writing it: **the security value of signing lives entirely in where the verifying key sits**, so a key the agent could rewrite is checksum-level protection wearing a signature's clothes and is invisible to any test; and **the threat is operational before it is adversarial**, since a cloned SD card, a wrong restore, and a cache from another installation each produce a file that is intact, passes a checksum, and is not ours.

**One rule was decided three times before anyone noticed it was one rule.** Discovery must never delete a node it does not see, because powered-off equipment is normal outside display hours and auto-deletion would remove healthy nodes for being asleep. That is Step 5's pruning decision (only a complete poll may prune) and ADR-011's stale-is-`unknown` rule, in a third disguise. **Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence**, now decided separately for telemetry, observations, and inventory. A fourth subsystem should inherit it rather than rediscover it.

Also available in parallel: RES-002's bench capture, which is the highest-risk record in the project and needs the physical rig, and `pkg/pjlink` at L1. RES-012 is blocked on projectors not currently being set up.

Two things a future session should know before implementing ADR-024, both of which are corrections of arguments the first draft made and two independent reviews demolished.

**An authorization refusal is not coordinator loss.** The draft argued that an identity failure leaves the operator in the same position as a coordinator outage, which the architecture requires to be survivable, and leaned on it twice. A coordinator outage is a **transport** failure, which is what an ADR-004 reduced local fallback detects and fires on. A `403` is a **successful conversation with a healthy coordinator that returns a refusal**, and nothing in ADR-004, ADR-016, or the FPP plugin treats that as a fallback condition. So a rotated scheduler token missed on the FPP host means the macro's coordinator-required steps and its locally executable steps both fail to run, which is strictly worse than the genuine outage. ADR-024 decision 7 makes `401` and `403` defined fallback triggers.

**The same error had a second disguise in the same record.** The draft required every write to be attributed and refused any command whose audit write failed, justified by "refusing new commands is what a coordinator outage already does, and the show survives it". The command being refused is blackout, and Phase 1 contains blackout. Every other degradation in this architecture points at *the show continuing*; an unqualified audit gate points at *the operator being unable to stop it*, and "the show survives it" is the wrong success criterion for a tripped eFuse or somebody at the door. The trigger is real rather than theoretical: ARCHITECTURE §11 names disk exhaustion, the Compose bundle rotates no logs for either container, and SQLite does not return freed pages without a vacuum. Blackout, stop, and power-off are now a named safety class that proceeds with degraded attribution; fail-closed is kept for `config:write` and `principal:write`.

The generalizable shape, worth carrying past this record: **an argument that degradation is safe, made against the wrong failure direction.** Degrading toward the show continuing and degrading toward the operator staying in control are different properties and need separate arguments.

Separately, the probe is ready to run against the real FPP player whenever the owner has bench time. That is what moves RES-002 from L1 to L2, and RES-002 is the highest-risk research record in the project.

The third-party product name discussed under "Conflicts found" in the audio session entry below had been removed from the working copy of `docs/reference-installation.md` but remained in the git history of the initial commit, and therefore on the remote, because removing a line from the working tree does not remove it from history. History was rewritten on 2026-08-10 to carry the neutral wording from the initial commit onward, every reachable object was re-scanned to confirm no blob or commit message still contains it, and the result was force-pushed. All commit hashes changed at that point; anything referencing a pre-rewrite hash is stale.

## 2026-08-14 (Track B seam B1: the node agent receives and acts on a command)

**Goal:** deliver Track B's B1 — the node agent subscribes to its own MQTT command topic, executes only an allowlisted operation, and reports the outcome as evidence, per ARCHITECTURE §10.4 ("agents accept only allowlisted operations," recorded in ADR-024's consequences as not yet delivered) and ADR-003 (a command is not successful because it was received). Branch `track-b/agent-foundation`, worktree `/Users/erbartos/Documents/code/showmesh-track-b`, branched from `docs/renderer-transport-adr` per the Track B spec. Orchestrated per CLAUDE.md's build workflow: this session wrote the spec and did not implement; a Sonnet subagent implemented; an Opus subagent reviewed against the named ADRs; findings were folded back and re-verified independently. GStreamer, media, NDI, FSEQ, the ADR-025 signed fallback cache, and any coordinator-side dispatcher were explicitly out of scope — this seam proves the agent's receiving half only, with one deliberately trivial allowlisted operation (`agent.echo`).

**Completed:**

- `pkg/mqttproto/payload.go`: `CmdPayload`/`ResultPayload`/`AgentEchoPayload` wire types (schemas `showmesh.node.cmd/v1`, `showmesh.node.result/v1`, `showmesh.node.agent.echo/v1`), each with `Validate()`, `Decode*Payload`, and `New*Envelope`, following the existing `HelloPayload`/`HealthPayload`/`LWTPayload` pattern exactly. Deliberately independent of `pkg/command.Envelope` rather than importing it — same field semantics, JSON-tagged separately — both because that package stays "deliberately thin" by its own doc comment and because Step 8 may be concurrently editing it on `main`; nothing outside `pkg/mqttproto`, `internal/agent`, and `test/integration` was touched. Stale doc comments in `payload.go`/`topic.go`/`doc.go` claiming "pkg/command is still a stub" and "no cmd/result payload type lives here yet" were corrected.
- `internal/agent/command.go`: the allowlist (`newOperationRegistry`, one entry today, `"agent.echo"`), the idempotency mechanism, and `CommandHandler.HandleMessage`, which validates topic/envelope/target/confirmation-method, checks idempotency, checks the deadline, executes, and always publishes a result — refusal included, never a silent drop, except for a structurally undecodable message with no trustworthy command ID.
- `internal/agent/mqtt.go`: the agent now subscribes to its own cmd topic and routes inbound publishes to the handler, wired inside the existing `OnConnectionUp` callback via `cm.AddOnPublishReceived`/`cm.Subscribe` so it survives reconnects — verified against the vendored `autopaho` v0.23.0 source rather than assumed.
- `test/integration/agent_command_test.go`: three tests against a real `showmesh-agent` subprocess and a real Mosquitto broker (`echo` confirms and is observed retained; a non-allowlisted action is refused; a redelivered idempotency key executes once).

**Decisions made:**

- **Wire types mirror `pkg/command.Envelope`'s field semantics without importing it.** This project's established idiom (per `cmd/showmeshctl`'s own import-graph enforcement and doc comments) is independent, JSON-tagged wire types at each boundary, reconciled by integration tests rather than by cross-package type sharing — applied here rather than inventing a new rule.
- **Evidence collection is a distinct step from execution, even when synchronous.** `agentEchoState` writes, then performs a separately-coded read-back before declaring an outcome confirmed, so the shape is right for a future asynchronous operation (e.g. a GStreamer pipeline reaching a running state) that must poll for its own evidence rather than trusting that a write call returning is sufficient. `OperationResult` carries `ExecutedAt` and `ObservedAt` as two distinct fields for the same reason, after review caught them aliased to one pointer in an earlier draft.
- **Idempotency is enforced as an atomic claim, not a check-then-act.** `idempotencyCache.claimOrAwait`/`complete` implement a hand-rolled singleflight rather than a separate `get` then `put`, because `HandleMessage` runs concurrently per inbound publish (one goroutine per message, so it can't block the MQTT read loop) — see Findings below for why this was not the first draft.

**Findings from review (Opus, given the diff plus CLAUDE.md, told to hunt for constraint violations and break the work rather than read it):**

- **SEVERE, confirmed empirically.** The first draft's idempotency cache was a plain `get`/`put` pair, which is two lock acquisitions with the operation executing in the gap — two concurrent deliveries of the same idempotency key could both miss the cache and both execute, making ADR-008's "a redelivered command executes exactly once" false under exactly the condition it exists for. The existing sequential redelivery test passed regardless, because it never created the race. The reviewer proved the double-execution deterministically before a fix existed. Fixed by the atomic claim above; a new test forces the concurrent interleaving deterministically (an operation held open by a channel until both goroutines have reached it, not a timing hope) and was confirmed to fail against the reintroduced bug and pass against the fix.
- **A test's name was a claim the test didn't support.** `TestHandleMessageMalformedPayloadDropsWithNoPublish` asserted "no publish happens" for a malformed payload, but removing the actual decode-error guard still produced no publish — for an unrelated reason further downstream (an empty command ID failing result-topic construction) — so the test passed with the guard it named entirely removed. Fixed by asserting the specific decode-failure log line instead of only the absence of a publish, and re-confirmed the fixed test now fails without the guard. This is the same "a test's name is a claim; break the behavior and confirm it fails" rule Step 3's review already established, holding on a fourth subsystem.
- Four smaller findings, all fixed: the confirmation-method literal's issuer was decoded and required by `Validate` but never logged (now logged); `RequestedRevision` was decoded but silently unenforced (now documented as such rather than left looking like it participates — the one allowlisted operation isn't revision-sensitive); the MQTT publish-received callback reported every inbound message as "handled" regardless of topic (now scoped, so a future second subscription doesn't get silently swallowed); `CmdPayload.Params` used `omitempty`, collapsing an absent key and an explicit empty object into the same wire value — this project's absent/null/empty distinction, now shipped correctly instead of as a fifth occurrence of the bug.
- **One additional defect, found by the implementer while chasing an integration-suite failure cascade, not by the reviewer:** the integration test's own setup called `provisionBrokerCredential(t, "coordinator")`, which rotates that shared role's broker password rather than fetching it, invalidating the credential for every other test running later in the same suite. Reproduced identically across two independent full-suite runs (~20 unrelated tests failing on `CONNACK 0x87 Not Authorized`) before being traced to this cause. Fixed by reusing the harness's already-seeded coordinator credential instead of rotating it.
- A second, unrelated collision was hit independently: two `make test-integration` invocations running concurrently in the same worktree (one from re-verification, one from the implementer) share the fixed container name `showmesh-test-mosquitto`, and one run's teardown removed the container out from under the other mid-suite, producing a wall of unrelated failures with no code cause at all. Not a code defect; recorded here because a future session hitting an identical-looking failure wall in this worktree should suspect a concurrent run before suspecting the diff.

**Deferred:** everything explicitly out of scope per the Track B spec — GStreamer pipeline supervision, NDI, FSEQ extraction, the ADR-025 signed fallback cache, and a coordinator-side API or UI to dispatch a command to a node (the integration test publishes directly to the broker for exactly this reason). `RequestedRevision` enforcement is deferred to whichever future operation is actually revision-sensitive; `agent.echo` is not. Capability advertisement for anything this seam adds is unchanged — B1 is receive-and-act only, not advertisement, per the Track B deliverable split.

**Verification gates:** `gofmt -l .` clean; `go vet ./...` clean; `go test ./pkg/mqttproto/... ./internal/agent/... -race -count=1` clean, including the new deterministic concurrency regression test; `go build`/cross-compile clean for `linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`, `darwin/arm64`, `windows/amd64` with `CGO_ENABLED=0`; `make test-integration` (real Mosquitto, real `showmesh-agent` and `showmesh-coordinator` subprocesses) clean at 90.8s in an uncontested solo run, including all three `TestAgentCommand*` tests. Nothing committed; the worktree stands ready for rebase and merge proposal against `track-b/agent-foundation`'s base.

## 2026-08-13 (Steps 8 and 9 sequenced, and a contradiction between four documents resolved)

**Goal:** close Step 7 in the repository rather than only in the working tree, then decide what comes next. No implementation.

**Completed:** the Step 7 loose-end work committed (`14e0e35`), and Steps 8 and 9 specified in BUILD-PLAN.

**The contradiction, because finding it was most of the work.** BUILD-LOG's current-state block, CLAUDE.md's prose, and CLAUDE.md's build order all said the next action was Step 8, the agent's GStreamer pipeline supervision into an NDI sink. BUILD-PLAN's "not yet sequenced" section listed that same work as **blocked** on RES-004 (unresearched, L0, critical), RES-005 (unresearched, L0, critical), and RES-006 (L1). All three were checked and all three still read that way. So three documents named a next action that the fourth said could not start, and CLAUDE.md's own rule says BUILD-PLAN wins any disagreement about a step. The working convention that architecture-critical claims need L3 before adoption says the same thing independently. That work is now sequenced after the bench that raises those records, and is described as a bench step whose product is evidence rather than an implementation step.

**Step 8 is the primitive command vocabulary, and the ordering was the owner's correction.** The first proposal was macros. The owner pointed out that Step 7 shipped one command out of a family, and that finishing the commands was the alternative. That is the better order, and ADR-004's own formulation says so: primitives, then macros, then reduced local fallback. A macro is a sequence of primitives and exactly one exists, the deliberately safe zero-argument stop, so the first macro would be a sequence of one or the primitives would get built inside the macro step. **Step 7 is the evidence for the second outcome**, having been specified as one write and shipped three. The macro step separately carries the plugin, RES-015's distribution question, ADR-024 decision 7, ADR-004's per-macro fallback definitions, and macro definitions as configuration objects, which is already more than one reviewable step.

**Two authorization decisions settled before Step 8 could be specified, both by the owner.**

**Target-scoped authorization is declined, not deferred.** ADR-024 decision 4 delivers authorization by action and explicitly not by target, leaving ARCHITECTURE §10.4 partially satisfied, and its supersession clause says a future record must revisit it "once there is a consumer to design its taxonomy against." Step 9's plugin credential technically is that consumer, since RES-015 §7.4 establishes that an FPP host cannot keep a secret from anyone who can reach it. The owner's decision is that this installation has no such need and will not acquire one: one operator, owned hardware, and a second person helping would be trusted with full control rather than issued a narrowed grant. **The distinction between declined and unmet is the whole point of recording it.** A future session reading ADR-024's supersession clause in Step 9 would otherwise see a stated trigger fire and reopen a question that has an answer. No ADR amendment, because re-affirming an existing deferral changes no constraint.

**`fpp:command` stays a single scope.** The alternative weighed was splitting the safe direction from the show-affecting one, so that Step 9's plugin credential could hold stop without holding start. The owner's argument against is that the role name already carries the meaning: `operator` means the principal operates the show, and starting it is operating it. The concern this was weighed against, that adding a start command silently widens every existing grant, does not survive a check of who holds the scope: only `operator` and `admin`, both of which should hold every command, while `viewer` holds no write scope and `scheduler` holds only `show:macro:run`. Nothing gains a capability its role did not already imply.

**Step 9 ships the plugin against the container, by the owner's decision**, on the same reasoning that has governed the bench since Step 1: a working system in a controlled environment first, hardware differences addressed when it lands there. Recorded with its limits rather than as a blanket, because RES-015 says every one of its acceptance criteria needs the bench Pi and the deployed fleet is not uniform. So Step 9 completes without raising RES-015 above L1, and the on-host install path, permissions, packaging, and cross-version compatibility are a stated deferral rather than a discovery.

**One accepted risk written into Step 9 rather than mitigated.** The plugin credential holds `fpp:command` in full and lives on a host that cannot keep it secret, so anyone reaching any FPP host has fleet-wide command authority. Accepted on the same grounds `SECURITY.md` already accepts cleartext on the show LAN. It is recorded so that the day this software runs somewhere with a crew, the accepted risk is findable rather than reconstructed.

**Documentation corrected.** BUILD-PLAN's Step 7 status now records the 08-13 repair, having read as though nothing had changed since the 08-12 verification. RES-008's status line no longer claims every decision it exists to make is undecided, which stopped being true when its own section 6a was written on 08-12 and was wrong once D1 and D2 shipped as code; its section 3 is marked stale at schema v6, with the re-run named as a blocking prerequisite for Step 9 per the record's own instruction that a stale survey claiming there is no configuration table is worse than no survey. The research tracker row is resynced.

**Two follow-ups after the step sections were written, both the owner's calls.**

**Step 8's filter must report its own exclusions.** The filter admits only commands whose effect the collector can already observe. The owner's addition is that every command excluded by it is listed with its reason, split by owner: those ShowMesh cannot yet confirm, which are candidates for a later step, and those FPP does not expose at all, which would need upstream FPP work and are out of scope for the foreseeable future. The argument is this project's own: a rule about absence, left unstated, is absence presented as nothing at all, which is the defect ADR-020's evidence vocabulary exists to prevent.

**RES-008 section 3 re-surveyed**, discharging Step 9's prerequisite; see the current-state block for what it found and what it now blocks.

**Deferred:** RES-002's bench captures, by the owner, to Sunday 2026-08-16. Not a blocker for Steps 8 or 9.

**Verification gates:** `gofmt`, `go vet`, and the full `go test ./...` clean before the commit; UI typecheck and 351 tests clean. No new code, so no acceptance criterion was touched.

## 2026-08-13 (The startup migration's failure direction)

**Goal:** fix the one Step 7 finding that was raised in review, judged correct, and left alone anyway: the `SHOWMESH_FPP_ENDPOINTS` to store migration failed closed on its audit write, so an unwritable `audit_log` meant the coordinator would not start at all. The owner agreed with the reviewer that this is the wrong failure direction.

**Completed:** `internal/coordinator/configsync.go`'s `migrateFPPEndpointsFromEnv` now logs at ERROR, persists nothing, returns the environment's endpoint list, and starts, for **both** failure modes `identity.Service.AuditedWrite` keeps distinguishable: the audit append failing (`identity.ErrAuditWrite`) and the config revision write itself failing (`fn`'s own error, returned unwrapped). The two are named apart in the message because their remedies differ. Three tests in `configsync_test.go` cover starting, returning the environment's list rather than nothing, persisting nothing, and completing the migration on a later boot.

**Why it was the wrong direction**, since the argument is the reusable part and is now in LESSONS.md. ADR-024 decision 11's fail-closed rule exists so an operator cannot act without a trace, and **a startup migration has no principal**, so refusing it protects nobody. Constraint 23 and decision 7 scope an identity or audit failure to "you cannot act", never "you cannot see"; exiting costs the reads, the writes, the API, the change stream, and the process at once. The shipped bundle sets `restart: unless-stopped`, so it is a restart loop rather than a stop. And the branch is reachable only on the first boot after an existing deployment upgrades into Step 7, which the operator would read as the upgrade having broken their coordinator. The same function already made the opposite call twice, eight lines above, for a zero `current_revision` and a dangling revision pointer, with a comment saying a store-integrity question must not become an availability outage.

**No ADR change, deliberately.** The fix exempts nothing from decision 11: `AuditedWrite` still rolls the whole transaction back, so the unattributable write still does not proceed. Only the process-level response changes, which belongs to constraint 13. Writing the revision anyway with degraded attribution, the posture seam C's blackout/stop/power-off safety class takes, **would** have been a second exemption to decision 11 and would have needed one; a configuration migration is not in that safety class, and retrying next boot costs nothing.

**The review found that the fix was incomplete in a way the fix itself created, and this is the part worth reading.** Making the failure non-fatal made a state reachable that had previously been impossible: *coordinator serving, `SHOWMESH_FPP_ENDPOINTS` set and in effect, store holding no `fpp.endpoints` configuration at all.* Before the deferral, the migration either created the object or the process exited, so no surface had ever needed an answer for it. Two had answers written under the old invariant, and both were now false.

`GET /api/v1/config/fpp.endpoints` answered `404` with *"no fpp.endpoints configuration has been created yet"*, and the Operator UI turned that into an empty table reading *"No `fpp.endpoints` configuration exists yet"*, while `GET /api/v1/fpp` listed every host being polled from the very list that failed to persist. That is ADR-020's own rejected alternative: a missing field renders as blank and blank reads as fine.

Worse, and closing with the operator making no mistake at any step: the `409` refusing a configuration write says *"Remove SHOWMESH_FPP_ENDPOINTS from this coordinator's environment and restart it once, then retry this write."* That is correct once a migration has landed, because removing the variable then leaves the migrated store configuration behind. While the migration is deferred there is no store configuration, so following the API's own written instruction resolves the coordinator to **zero endpoints**, and the retried write then fails on the same unwritable store. The pre-fix behavior was a loud restart loop; this would have been a quiet total loss of FPP observability reached by obeying the coordinator.

Both are fixed by threading the deferral through as data (`api.Dependencies.FPPEndpointsMigrationDeferred`, the same pattern `FPPEndpointsEnvVarSet` already uses so the API package still reads neither the environment nor the store's startup history). The read handler states the deferral and points at `GET /api/v1/fpp` for what is actually in effect; the write refusal keeps the same `409` and swaps in a non-destructive remedy that begins **"Do NOT remove SHOWMESH_FPP_ENDPOINTS"**; and the UI renders the coordinator's own detail verbatim instead of authoring its own sentence, because one of the two facts that `404` now carries is a warning.

**The review also caught the fix's own log line making a false causal claim** ("the store holds no configuration, **so** PUT stays refused with 409"). The `409` is caused solely by the variable being set and fires identically after a successful migration, so the sentence implied the refusal would lift once the migration landed. Corrected, along with a doc comment calling the deferred state "a coherent pre-migration posture", which the two findings above disprove.

**And it rejected the new tests' fake, correctly.** The first version overrode `identity.Service.AuditedWrite` to fail. The assertion those tests exist to make is that *nothing is persisted*, and the reason that holds is decision 11's same-transaction rule inside the real `AuditedWrite`. A fake that substitutes its own transaction proves that property about the fake: rewriting `AuditedWrite` to commit `fn`'s work and append the audit row separately, a direct violation of decision 11, would have left them green. They now install a real `BEFORE INSERT ... RAISE(ABORT)` trigger on `audit_log` or `config_revisions` over a second connection to the store's own SQLite file, which is both a truer fault and the same mechanism as the real-binary verification. One of the two also turned out to be testing a state unreachable in production, since `syncFPPEndpointsConfig` only calls `migrateFPPEndpointsFromEnv` on `ErrConfigObjectNotFound`.

**Decisions made:** two boundaries drawn rather than assumed. `DecodeFPPEndpointsPayload` failing on a corrupt stored payload still exits, and so does a non-`NotFound` error reading the config object; the latter is in the same family as `store.Open` failing, which `coordinator.go` makes deliberately fatal with a comment telling future sessions not to soften it. Both were raised with the owner and scoped out. `reportDeferredFPPEndpointsMigration` deliberately does **not** also write to stderr the way seam C's degraded-attribution report does: that one exists because an unattributed state change really happened and the audit row that would have recorded it is gone, so stderr is the substitute record. Here nothing was persisted, so this is a diagnostic rather than a record.

**A test written in the same commit as its code still lied, and mutation caught it.** `TestSyncFPPEndpointsConfigAuditWriteFailureStartsWithoutMigrating` asserted the log named the audit failure mode apart from a plain store failure by looking for `"audit entry could not be written"`. That phrase **also appears in `identity.ErrAuditWrite`'s own text**, which the log line attaches as its error field, so the assertion passed whether or not the two modes were distinguished at all. Replacing the cause clause with `MUTANT` left the test green. The distinguishing wording is now unique to the message, and both cause clauses were re-mutated to confirm each fails exactly the test that claims it. This project's "a test's name is a claim" rule usually catches old tests; here it caught one an hour old.

**Verification gates:** `gofmt`, `go vet`, and the full `go test ./...` clean; the UI's `typecheck`, `lint`, and all 351 tests clean. Mutation: the three coordinator tests all fail when the fix is reverted to `return nil, err`, and each of the two cause clauses fails exactly its own test.

Then, per the standing rule that the suite proves nothing on its own, **against a real coordinator binary with a genuinely unwritable `audit_log`**, twice. The first pass proved the failure direction: the binary built from `HEAD` exits **1**, the fixed binary starts, stays up, serves `GET /api/v1/fpp` with both configured instances, and leaves `config_objects`, `config_revisions` and `audit_log` at **zero rows**; dropping the trigger and restarting completes the migration with revision 1, source `env_migration`, and exactly one `config.migrate` audit entry with no principal.

The second pass, after the review, bootstrapped a real administrator with the `bootstrap` subcommand and minted a real API token so the two corrected messages could be read the way an operator reads them. In the deferred state, `GET /api/v1/config/fpp.endpoints` returns the `404` that states the deferral and points at `GET /api/v1/fpp`, and `PUT` returns the `409` titled *"the startup migration of SHOWMESH_FPP_ENDPOINTS was deferred"* whose detail begins *"Do NOT remove SHOWMESH_FPP_ENDPOINTS yet"*. The control was run in the same session: with the trigger dropped and the coordinator restarted, `GET` returns revision 1 from `env_migration` with both endpoints, and `PUT`'s refusal reverts to the standard remedy. `/readyz` is 503 throughout because no broker was running in the scratch environment, which is correct and unrelated.

**Not verified:** anything about a running show. No live fleet, no MQTT publish, no broker. Step 8 was still unspecified at the time of this entry, and was specified later the same day; see the entry above, which also changes what Step 8 is.
